findings.headline: Auditors commit to structured recovery with unmodified opinion targeted for 2027/28, subject to council delivering required support and resources
findings.detail: The auditors outline a detailed build-back programme with clear opinion milestones: modified or except-for opinion anticipated for 2026/27, and unmodified opinion for 2027/28. Success depends on completion of planned testing procedures and the council ensuring its finance function is adequately resourced, provides quality supporting evidence in response to audit queries, and makes key officers available to address audit requests on agreed timescales.
findings.matters: This demonstrates a structured and sequenced path to recovery of audit credibility and clean financial statements, contingent on specific council actions. For lenders and finance directors, it shows the audit issues are remediable if conditions are met—though delivery is conditional on external cooperation.
findings.figures: 2026/27: modified/except-for opinion (anticipated); 2027/28: unmodified opinion (anticipated)
findings.quote: We are committed to working with you to deliver this, and to move to the position of being able to issue an unmodified opinion on the Council's financial statements for the 2027/28 financial year

findings.headline: Target clean opinion date falls only three days before local government reorganisation takes effect
findings.detail: The auditors anticipate being able to issue an unmodified (clean) opinion for the year ended 31 March 2028. However, local government reorganisation is scheduled for 1 April 2028, leaving only a three-day window. Any slippage in the build-back plan risks the council merging into a new authority without clean audited accounts.
findings.matters: This creates significant deadline risk: delays in the recovery plan could result in the council failing to achieve a clean opinion before reorganisation. It also creates time pressure that could affect the quality of audit work or the council's ability to meet intermediate milestones.
findings.figures: Target opinion date: 31 March 2028; Reorganisation effective date: 1 April 2028
findings.quote: achieve a clean opinion prior to Local Government reorganisation on 1 April 2028

findings.headline: Risk assessment identifies council at higher end of audit risk spectrum, requiring extensive testing of income and expenditure across the disclaimed period
findings.detail: The auditors' detailed risk assessment concluded the council is at the higher end of the risk spectrum for build-back assurance. The assessment examined qualitative factors including control environment strength, reserve complexity, changes in key personnel and systems, and issues reported by internal audit. The high-risk rating drives the need for extensive substantive procedures over income and expenditure transactions during the four disclaimed years.
findings.matters: A high-risk assessment indicates systemic issues in the council's financial management, controls, or reporting quality during the disclaimed period. This affects lender confidence in the council's financial governance and explains the substantial cost and scope of the recovery work.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Our risk assessment has concluded that the Council is at the higher end of the risk spectrum for build back assurance. This means extensive procedures over the Council's income and expenditure transactions will be required over the disclaimed period.

findings.headline: Finance function capacity constraints prevented planned audit work in 2024/25, deferring majority of testing to 2025/26 and 2026/27
findings.detail: The auditors report they were unable to complete planned build-back audit procedures in 2024/25 due to capacity challenges within the finance function, combined with historical audit delays. As a result, the majority of detailed testing has been deferred, creating risk to the timeline for recovery.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity is essential to supporting both routine audits and specialized build-back testing. Ongoing constraints could jeopardize the auditors' target timeline of achieving a clean opinion by 2027/28, and indicate staffing or resourcing pressures within the council.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: we were unable to complete planned build back audit procedures in 2024/25 due to a combination of factors, including historical audit delays, and capacity challenges within the finance function

findings.matters: These are material additional costs drawn from the council's budget. For lenders, the cost magnitude reflects the severity and complexity of audit remediation required. For finance directors, it represents a significant allocation of budget to audit work.

findings.matters: Lenders cannot assess the council's true financial position; finance directors cannot have confidence in reported reserves or account balances. This undermines creditworthiness and financial stewardship across five financial years.

findings.detail: The council achieved £0.691m favorable outturn on treasury management. Investment income reached £1.505m against budget of £1.000m (£0.505m outperformance). Interest payments on loans came in £0.186m under budget at £3.083m actual v £3.269m budgeted. However, with Bank Rate now at 3.75% and held stable per MPC guidance, and Arlingclose forecasting rates to remain at 3.75%, the elevated investment returns achieved during the year (when rates were higher) are unlikely to recur.
findings.matters: A lender would note that the favorable treasury surplus appears driven by timing of high interest rates during the year, not sustainable income generation. Council budgets may need revision if investment income declines materially in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Council holds £12.3m in commercial and property investments purchased for yield and is divesting before taking new borrowing.
findings.detail: The council holds £4.3m of commercial investments plus £8m being marketed for sale, purchased before CIPFA Prudential Code changes prohibited borrowing to invest primarily for financial return. The council has explicitly stated it will review exit options 'before undertaking further additional borrowing'. Two property funds have already wound down, returning £9.9m. Non-treasury subsidiary investments of £5.0m (shareholdings £1.7m, loans £3.3m) generated only 2.8% return (£0.143m income).
findings.matters: A lender would see this as the council realigning away from leveraged investment strategies and back towards alignment with current prudential code. Successful divestment of these assets could materially improve the council's net borrowing position.

findings.headline: Borrowing of £59.0m exceeds the prudent liability benchmark of £39.1m by £19.9m; long-term borrowing is on hold pending rate improvement.
findings.detail: The council's external borrowing sits £19.9m above the liability benchmark (which estimates minimum borrowing needed to fund planned capex while maintaining £5m minimum liquidity). The council has explicitly paused long-term borrowing due to high PWLB rates: 10-year maturity rose from 5.38% at April 2025 to 5.72% at year-end, well above Bank Rate of 3.75%. The council expects future rate reductions. The gap between borrowing and benchmark has narrowed from £31.8m (2025) to £19.9m (2026).
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about borrowing above prudent levels, though the narrowing trend suggests improving discipline. The rate environment is also material—frozen long-term borrowing could indicate either prudent timing or deferred capital spending.
findings.figures: Liability benchmark £39.1m; Actual borrowing £59.0m; Gap £19.9m (vs £31.8m prior year); 10-year PWLB rate: 1 April 5.38% → 31 March 5.72%; Bank Rate: 4.50% → 3.75%
findings.quote: The Authority's short-term borrowing has continued, as entering into any longer-term debt is on hold, due to long term PWLB interest rates remaining high.

findings.headline: 97.46% of the £59.0m borrowing portfolio matures within 12 months, concentrated in £50m of short-term PWLB loans.
findings.detail: The council's debt is heavily skewed to short-term maturity with only £1.5m long-term fixed borrowing (8.875%, 29-year maturity). The £50m of short-term PWLB loans carry a 4.85% average rate and will be replaced with inter-local authority borrowing on maturity. This concentration exposes the council to material refinancing risk if capital markets deteriorate or short-term rates spike when these loans are rolled over.
findings.matters: A lender would assess refinancing risk; if short-term rates rise materially, the council's cost of borrowing could increase significantly at point of maturity. The reliance on inter-local authority lending for renewal also creates counterparty concentration risk.
findings.figures: Maturity structure: under 12 months 97.46%, 10+ years 2.54%; Short-term PWLB £50m at 4.85% average; Long-term PWLB £1.5m at 8.875%
findings.quote: The average rate on the Authority's short-term PWLB loans of £50m, as at 31st March 2026 was 4.85%, these will be replaced with inter local authority borrowing on maturity.

findings.headline: Net borrowing increased from £30.4m to £34.9m as investment balances fell by £10.0m.

Long-term treasury investments were eliminated entirely (from £9.9m to nil) following wind-down of two property funds. The council is consuming resources faster than reducing debt, indicating worsening underlying financial position.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council is drawing down its cash reserves even while reducing gross borrowing, suggesting it may be in structural deficit and could require additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Net borrowing: 31.3.25 £30.4m → 31.3.26 £34.9m (increase £4.5m); Total investments: £34.1m → £24.1m (decrease £10.0m); Long-term investments: £9.9m → £0

findings.paper_title: Update on Assets of Community Value
findings.headline: New Sporting ACV regime could indefinitely restrict hundreds of council sports facilities, with unclear listing criteria and guidance pending.

findings.paper_title: Update on Assets of Community Value

findings.matters: A £245k unbudgeted expense represents a material revenue pressure on the council's finances, directly resulting from its failure to maintain adequate audit trail and account balances in prior years.

findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion signals that the council's financial statements cannot be relied upon, which is fundamental information for lenders assessing creditworthiness and for the finance director managing the council's finances.
findings.quote: The Council has received a disclaimed audit opinion for the years 2021/22 to 2024/25, the audit will present the Build-back plan (as attached at Appendix B). This sets out the proposed approach by the auditors to build back assurance on the Councils balances.

findings.headline: Liquid investment balances fell 29% as the council depleted reserves to reduce debt
findings.detail: Balance sheet resources (the council's investment/cash balances) fell from £34.1m to £24.1m, a £10m reduction. Capital receipts were used to pay down short-term borrowing rather than rebuild reserves. While the property fund return of £12.8m was planned and positive, the net effect is a significantly depleted cash cushion.
findings.matters: At the same time as the council is concentrating refinancing risk (97% of debt under 12 months) and deferring long-term borrowing on a bet that rates fall, it is also reducing its financial buffers. If capital receipts dry up or unexpected pressures arise, the council has less liquidity to absorb shocks without new borrowing.
findings.figures: Balance sheet resources down £10.0m (29% reduction), property funds returned £12.8m, net borrowing increased from £30.4m to £34.9m despite external debt falling
findings.quote: Short-term borrowing reduced, as in year capital receipts were used to offset borrowing.

findings.headline: £4.3m commercial property investments constrain future borrowing options under new CIPFA rules
findings.detail: The council holds £4.3m in commercial investments (shareholdings and loans to subsidiaries) plus £8m more currently being marketed for sale, all originally purchased for financial return before the 2021 CIPFA Prudential Code banned councils from borrowing to invest for yield. The authority explicitly states it will not undertake further borrowing until these are exited.
findings.matters: These legacy investments are a constraint on future capital flexibility. Until they are sold, they prevent the council from using standard borrowing instruments and tie up capital that could otherwise service debt. Sale delays or shortfalls could force difficult choices.
findings.figures: £4.3m held in subsidiaries, £8m being marketed for sale, 2.8% rate of return on subsidiary investments
findings.quote: The Authority currently holds £4.3m in commercial investments plus a further £8m currently being marketed for sale that were primarily purchased for financial return prior to the change in the CIPFA Prudential Code. Before undertaking further additional borrowing the Authority will review the options for exiting these investments.

findings.headline: Long-term borrowing deferred while betting PWLB rates will fall below 5.72%
findings.detail: The council has deferred all new longer-term borrowing while PWLB 10-year certainty rates sit at 5.72% (up from 5.38% a year earlier). The treasury strategy states 'entering into any longer-term debt is on hold, due to long term PWLB interest rates remaining high.' This is a bet that rates will fall before the council needs to lock in long-term debt.
findings.matters: If PWLB rates stay elevated or rise, this leaves the council forced to keep refinancing at short-term rates (currently 5-7%), with no option to lock in. Every year the council waits, the risk of having to accept higher long-term rates increases.
findings.figures: PWLB 10-year rate 5.72% at 31 March (vs 5.38% at 1 April), £50m PWLB short-term at 4.85% average rate, weighted average maturity 3.5 months
findings.quote: The Authority's short-term borrowing has continued, as entering into any longer-term debt is on hold, due to long term PWLB interest rates remaining high.

findings.headline: Nearly all borrowing (97%) matures within 12 months, creating annual refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council's £59m borrowing portfolio is concentrated in short-term debt: £50m PWLB and £7.5m inter-local authority loans, both due within 3-4 months. This forces the council to refinance almost its entire borrowing annually. At year-end, short-term rates spiked to 5-7%, up from 4-4.5% earlier.
findings.matters: This maturity profile exposes the council to refinancing risk: if rates remain elevated or tighten further, rolling over £57m of maturing debt annually could blow the budget. There is no certainty costs will be stable.
findings.figures: £57.5m short-term borrowing (97.46% of total), short-term rates 5.0%-7.0% at year-end vs 4.0%-4.5% earlier, 4-month weighted average maturity
findings.quote: The cost of short-term borrowing from other local authorities has been similar to or a little above Base Rate for most of the period, with interest rates between 4.0% and 4.5%. However, as is commonly seen, rates rose higher towards the end of the financial year, with rates of 5.0% - 7.0% being seen.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Risk Register 2026-27 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation to single unitary authority on 1 April 2028 creates significant implementation risk including one-off transition costs
findings.detail: Government confirmed on 16 July 2026 that Hertfordshire will reorganise into four unitary authorities, with East Herts forming part of the new East Hertfordshire and Broxbourne unitary. The transition creates significant implementation risk including additional one-off costs, pressure on senior officer and service capacity, disruption to business-as-usual delivery, uncertainty for staff, and potential loss of key skills. The council's Medium Term Financial Plan includes financial planning for potential one-off costs, and the council notes it will maintain adequate reserves to manage transition costs where possible.
findings.matters: Major structural reorganisation creates implementation risk and one-off costs that will affect council capacity and financial resilience during the transition period to April 2028
findings.figures: Transition date 1 April 2028; elections to shadow authorities May 2027; specific one-off cost amount not disclosed
findings.quote: The transition to the new arrangements creates significant implementation risk, including additional one-off costs, pressure on senior officer and service capacity, disruption to business-as-usual delivery, uncertainty for staff, potential loss of key skills, competing demands on organisational focus, and risks to financial planning and governance during the period to vesting day on 1 April 2028.

Monthly updates on 12 KPIs including forecast, income, net income, occupancy, ticket sales and spend per head are now being reported to executive, senior leadership team and portfolio holders.

findings.quote: £348K overspend in Parking, driven by higher business rates pressure, which has been resolved for 2026/27, and the cleansing contract which is under review and options to be considered for managing ongoing pressure.

findings.matters: Shows late-emerging cost pressures on major assets and contractor relationships that should have been forecastable, indicating weak asset management or procurement controls.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Outturn 2025/26 and Draft Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: General Fund balance sits only £0.205M above the calculated minimum, leaving almost no headroom
findings.detail: The General Fund balance is £3.854M against a calculated minimum of £3.649M. This leaves only £0.205M of unallocated headroom to absorb any unexpected financial shock. Combined with the £2.038M annual earmarked reserve drawdown, the council has minimal financial resilience.
findings.matters: Minimal headroom means any significant unexpected cost (a service failure, a contract dispute, an asset write-down) would force the council to either cut services immediately or breach its minimum reserve policy.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Outturn 2025/26 and Draft Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves depleted by £2.038M in a single year to cover multiple pressures
findings.detail: The council drew £2.038M from earmarked reserves in 2025/26 to fund operational pressures including £986K for service delivery costs (waste contract mobilisation, LG reorganisation, redundancies, grounds maintenance) and £678K for the revenue overspend itself. This rate of reserve depletion is unsustainable.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown of this scale indicates the council is using one-off reserves to fund recurring operational problems rather than fixing them structurally. At this rate earmarked reserves will be exhausted within a decade.
findings.figures: £2.038M earmarked reserves used; earmarked reserves now £15.259M (down from £17.297M); includes £986K service pressures, £678K overspend, £240K Lothbury property fund loss, £133K business rates smoothing
findings.quote: In 2025/26, a net £2.038M was transferred from the Council's Earmarked Reserves, with the main areas of reserve usage being: £986K to fund expenditure within the Net Cost of Services, including mobilisation costs of the new waste contract, costs associated with Local Government reorganisation, redundancies, volatility in the housing benefits budget and increased costs against the grounds maintenance contract; £678K to fund the 2025/26 revenue overspend

findings.paper_title: Provisional Outturn 2025/26 and Draft Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: BEAM service significantly overran budget by £1.167M and deteriorated sharply
findings.detail: The BEAM service overspent by £1.167M driven by lower income and higher staffing and operating costs. This represented a £709K worsening from the Q3 forecast, suggesting the underlying cost pressures accelerated in the final quarter and were not effectively managed.
findings.matters: BEAM is the single largest driver of the overall overspend and the £709K adverse movement from Q3 suggests cost control problems within this service. A lender needs to understand what BEAM is and why it is uncontrollable.
findings.figures: £1.167M overspend; £709K worse than Q3 forecast
findings.quote: £1.167M net overspend on BEAM (a £709K adverse movement from quarter 3) reflecting lower income and higher staffing and operating costs.

findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £678K funded from earmarked reserves
findings.detail: The council exceeded its revenue budget by £678K in 2025/26 and was forced to cover this from earmarked reserves rather than absorbing it within budget. The overspend came on top of variances across multiple service areas and reduces the council's financial cushion.
findings.matters: Shows the council cannot reliably balance its budget within the financial year and must draw on reserves to cover overspends, reducing its flexibility for future pressures.
findings.figures: £678K overspend; funded from £2.038M total earmarked reserve drawdown
findings.quote: An overspend of £678K is reported against the 2025/26 revenue budget. In line with the Council's financial procedure rules the Director for Finance, Risk & Performance has approved that the overspend be funded from the general reserve.

findings.headline: Capital programme underspend of £3.3m (27% of budget) with £1.1m carry-forward indicates significant project slippage
findings.detail: More than one quarter of the capital budget remains unspent, with major items deferred: £392k operational assets investment not started, £250k contingency unused, £70k parks project not actioned. While deferrals are normal, the scale here suggests challenges in executing the planned programme within the financial year.
findings.matters: A pattern of capital slippage can indicate poor planning, delivery capacity issues, or external constraints; lenders need confidence the council can execute its investment strategy
findings.figures: Total budget £11,925k, outturn £8,628k, variance (£3,297k), carry-forward £1,142k
findings.quote: Current Capital Programme Budget Total 11,925 [budget] 8,628 [outturn] (3,297) [variance] 1,142 [carry forward]

findings.headline: Website replacement project claimed overspend does not align with reported budget figures
findings.detail: The commentary states the BEAM website outturn is £9k over budget, yet the budget table shows £51k budgeted and £51k outturn with zero variance. This is a reporting discrepancy that either indicates cost control issues or data entry errors, and needs clarification on what the actual cost was and whether it truly overran.
findings.matters: Cost control and accurate financial reporting are material to lender confidence; unexplained discrepancies between commentary and figures suggest either control weaknesses or reporting problems
findings.figures: Budget £51k, Outturn £51k shown in table; commentary claims £9k overspend
findings.quote: Outturn is £9k over budget.

findings.headline: Buntingford depot EV infrastructure planning application rejected, seeking alternatives
findings.detail: A planning application for structural changes at Amwell failed. The council is now actively seeking alternative delivery routes for the EV infrastructure project. This represents a real setback to a capital scheme, though the project itself is small.
findings.matters: Capital delivery risk is a real concern for lenders; failed planning can delay projects and increase costs, and it shows whether the council can successfully execute its capital strategy
findings.figures: £10k additional contingency allocated at Buntingford for completed works; planning failure at Amwell location
findings.quote: Planning application for structural changes at Amwell was unsuccessful. Officers to seek alternatives opportunities.

findings.headline: Fitness membership fell by 312 users, with facility problems and disruption explicitly cited as cause
findings.detail: Membership base contracted from 10,421 to 10,109. Report states: 'The reduction has also been influenced by operational factors, including issues with shower and changing facilities at Hartham, and disruption associated with the gym refurbishment at Grange Paddocks.' This indicates member losses directly traceable to poor facility condition.
findings.matters: Direct evidence that operational problems are causing measurable revenue loss from core membership base
findings.figures: 312-user reduction; 3% decline from 10,421 to 10,109
findings.quote: The reduction has also been influenced by operational factors, including issues with shower and changing facilities at Hartham, and disruption associated with the gym refurbishment at Grange Paddocks.

findings.headline: Hartham swimming satisfaction collapsed from 80.9% to 67.7% due to facility problems
findings.detail: Sharp 13.2 percentage-point decline in customer satisfaction at Hartham's swimming facilities directly attributed to shower boiler failures and contractor delays closing changing village. Overall gym satisfaction also fell from 85.2% to 83.2%.
findings.matters: Service quality decline directly impacts revenue and membership, with problems traced to facility management failures
findings.figures: Hartham swimming: 80.9% to 67.7%; gym and group exercise: 85.2% to 83.2%
findings.quote: At Hartham, satisfaction scores fell from 80.9% in 2024 to 67.7% in 2025, largely due to ongoing issues with the shower boiler systems.

findings.headline: Electricity consumption at Hartham increased 66% following refurbishment, representing material cost increase
findings.detail: Shift to air source heat pump for refurbished areas caused 66% year-on-year increase in electricity consumption. Gas consumption increased 4.71% across both sites. Report acknowledges 'further reviews by EA are ongoing to identify where additional efficiencies can be achieved', indicating costs remain unresolved.
findings.matters: Significant unplanned operational cost increase that will be ongoing; suggests capital decisions produced higher-cost operational outcomes than anticipated
findings.figures: Hartham electricity up 66% year-on-year; gas up 4.71% across contract
findings.quote: Hartham recorded a 66% year on year increase in electricity consumption, reflecting the significant change in the size and operational mix of the facility.

findings.headline: Hartham leisure facility refurbishment systems have failed, requiring replacement and further capital investment
findings.detail: Shower boiler systems installed during refurbishment proved unreliable and required complete replacement in June 2025. Air source heat pump required emergency temporary replacement in January. Changing village closed for one month in October due to delayed contractor availability. The report explicitly states feedback resulted in 'the need for a further refurbishment' of these same facilities.
findings.matters: Recent capital investment failing to deliver durable solutions; indicates either poor project oversight, contractor quality issues, or building defects requiring additional spending
findings.figures: No spend figures provided, but systems replaced in June and January; contractor delays in October
findings.quote: The units installed during refurbishment proved unreliable and required frequent repairs before being fully replaced in June as part of a new shower installation.

findings.headline: Committee has not requested officers to attend meetings to explain risks and audit findings
findings.detail: Committee members know they can request officers and risk owners to attend meetings but have not done so. Risks and audit findings are discussed only with the Audit Manager and Chief Finance Officer, not with the operational officers responsible for managing those risks.
findings.matters: When a committee doesn't directly question the officers responsible for managing risks or failing audits, it cannot properly test whether problems are being addressed or understand their severity. This reduces the committee's ability to escalate genuine concerns.
findings.figures: Scored 3/5 on Question 24; officers are 'open to questions and able to respond immediately' when they do attend
findings.quote: A&G Committee members are aware they can ask for Officers to attend Committee but have yet to request this.

findings.headline: Committee has not formally evaluated members' knowledge and skills
findings.detail: No formal evaluation of the knowledge, skills, or training needs of the Chair or committee members has been done in the last two years. Training is provided on key topics (Internal Audit, Fraud, Treasury, Risk) but is not based on a structured assessment of what capabilities the committee actually needs.
findings.matters: If committee members lack expertise in treasury management, accounting standards, or pensions liability, they cannot effectively challenge management on complex financial matters or spot emerging problems. This weakens the council's financial governance.
findings.figures: Scored 0/5 on Question 15; committee members are elected councillors with political balance maintained
findings.quote: No formal evaluation of the knowledge, skills or training needs of the Chair and Audit Committee members has been carried out within the last two years.

findings.headline: Audit Committee has not met privately with external auditors or internal audit manager
findings.detail: The Committee has not held private meetings with either the external auditors or the internal audit manager. CIPFA guidance specifically recommends this as essential practice so auditors can share sensitive findings that may not be discussed in public sessions. This gap means the committee may not be fully aware of audit concerns or control issues.
findings.matters: Private auditor meetings are where auditors escalate financial control problems that they cannot easily raise in public. Without them, governance weaknesses or financial risks could remain hidden from leadership and therefore from lenders assessing the council's financial health.
findings.figures: Scored 0/5 on Question 12; CIPFA 2022 guidance identifies this as a standard best practice
findings.quote: The Audit Committee have not met in private with the external auditors or head of internal audit (Audit Manager).

Homelessness is a statutory demand-led service where control failure could lead to uncontrolled budget exposure.
findings.matters: Homelessness is demand-led spending with limited ability to control volume. Unimplemented high-priority recommendations suggest management has not yet addressed fundamental control weaknesses in a service area where cost overruns can appear suddenly and be difficult to arrest.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditors Audit Plan 2025/26
findings.headline: Multiple significant risks in high-value asset and pension valuations with material estimation uncertainty
findings.detail: Identified as significant risks: land and buildings valuation (rolling five-year revaluation with indexation), investment property valuations (full annual revaluation), and defined benefit pension net liability (IAS 19). All assessed as high inherent risk, involve external RICS valuers or actuaries, and are sensitive to changes in key assumptions (discount rates, inflation, mortality, market conditions).
findings.matters: Large material balances involving high subjective estimation create audit complexity, potential for material misstatement, and balance sheet volatility that affects financial position assessment.
findings.figures: Overall materiality £1,518k (Council) set at 2% of gross revenue expenditure; Performance materiality £910k (60% of overall); these valuations represent significant components of the balance sheet
findings.quote: This represents a key accounting estimate made by management within the financial statements due to the size of the values involved, the subjectivity of the measurement and the sensitive nature of the estimate to changes in key assumptions. We have therefore identified the valuation of operational land and buildings as a significant risk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditors Audit Plan 2025/26
findings.headline: Statutory backstop date 31 January 2027: further disclaimer likely if audit procedures incomplete
findings.detail: The Code of Audit Practice 2024 requires auditors to issue their report by the backstop date even if audit procedures are incomplete, which will result in a disclaimer of opinion. This is the fourth consecutive year operating under backstop deadlines. Auditors acknowledge significant additional work is required to build back assurance.
findings.matters: Even if the council meets the 31 January 2027 deadline, a further disclaimer opinion will be issued if audit work cannot be completed, perpetuating lack of audit assurance and credit uncertainty.
findings.figures: Backstop date: 31 January 2027; additional audit fees for building back assurance, enhanced disclaimer reporting and VFM local government reorganisation work marked 'TBC'
findings.quote: The Code of Audit Practice 2024 specifies that auditors are required to issue their auditor's report before these dates, even if planned audit procedures are not fully complete, so that local government bodies can comply with the statutory reporting deadline. Where audit work is not complete, this will give rise to a disclaimer of opinion.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditors Audit Plan 2025/26
findings.headline: Revenue expenditure risk: systematic misclassification as capital would understate revenue spending
findings.detail: Auditors have brought forward from the predecessor auditor a high-risk area where revenue expenditure may be inappropriately capitalised either at posting or through end-of-year journal transfers. This has not been subject to audit procedures in previous years. If occurring, it would understate revenue expenditure and overstate property, plant and equipment additions.
findings.matters: Systematic misclassification of revenue as capital expenditure distorts the reported revenue budget position and overstates the capital asset base, potentially masking deteriorating revenue sustainability.
findings.figures: Inherent risk of material misstatement assessed as High for capitalisation of revenue expenditure
findings.quote: We have brought forward this risk from the predecessor auditor, as no audit procedures were undertaken in this area in previous years. We have assessed that the risk of misstatement of revenue outturn in the financial statements is most likely to be achieved through: Revenue expenditure being inappropriately recognised as capital expenditure at the point it is posted to the general ledger

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditors Audit Plan 2025/26
findings.headline: Finance team capacity constraints affecting audit delivery and recovery of audit assurance
findings.detail: Auditors identify finance team capacity as critical to delivering the audit and building back assurance by 2028. A 2024/25 recommendation to reassess roles, responsibilities and resource requirements remains open and in progress. Finance roles are currently under restructure; monthly meetings between CFO and leadership have been established to focus on financial requirements.
findings.matters: Insufficient finance team capacity risks further delays in audit completion, missed statutory deadlines, and failure to recover audit assurance by 2028, perpetuating financial reporting uncertainty.
findings.figures: Finance capacity recommendation from 2024/25 remains open; restructure of finance roles ongoing; monthly oversight meetings established
findings.quote: There is progress; however, implementing this recommendation is key if the Council is to continue to produce accounts on time and, moreover, have sufficient capacity to facilitate the annual audit and the additional audit work required to build back assurance and lift the disclaimer by 2028.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditors Audit Plan 2025/26
findings.headline: Significant weaknesses in governance arrangements for financial statement preparation and publication
findings.detail: The council did not produce financial statements in line with Accounts and Audit Regulations and omitted required website notices in 2023/24. Although the council has begun responding to statutory recommendations from April 2025, the response period has been insufficient for full implementation. The weakness remains a planned focus area in the 2025/26 audit.
findings.matters: Inability to produce timely, compliant financial statements on the first attempt raises questions about control environment, financial reporting reliability, and management capability that lenders depend on for credit decisions.
findings.figures: Statutory recommendations issued April 2025; weakness carried forward from 2024/25; 2024/25 accounts eventually published on time
findings.quote: There are significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements for the preparation and publication of financial statements. In 2023/24, the Council did not produce its financial statements in line with the Accounts and Audit regulations and did not include the required notices on its website.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditors Audit Plan 2025/26
findings.headline: Four consecutive disclaimed audit opinions; recovery work required to lift disclaimer by March 2028
findings.detail: Disclaimed opinions were issued for 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25. Auditors assess the council as 'at the higher end of the risk spectrum for building back assurance', requiring full procedures over income and expenditure transactions across all disclaimed years. Recovery targeted for 2027/28, subject to management implementing all recommendations and no adverse findings emerging.
findings.matters: Four years without audit assurance over financial statements creates fundamental uncertainty over the council's financial position and control environment that directly affects lender credit assessment.
findings.figures: Four consecutive years of disclaimed opinions (2021/22–2024/25); backstop dates: 31 January 2027 for 2025/26 accounts
findings.quote: Disclaimed opinions were issued by the predecessor auditor for 2021/22 and 2022/23 and by Azets in 2023/24 and 2024/25. Following the publication of LARRIGs 01 to 06 we have developed an overarching strategy for building back assurance for the Council, with the aim of recovering assurance by 31 March 2028.

findings.headline: Two audit areas received Limited Assurance: Old River Lane and Homelessness
findings.detail: Of 23 audits in 2025/26, nine received Substantial Assurance, eight Reasonable, and two Limited Assurance. The two Limited Assurance findings were for Old River Lane and Homelessness. Internal audit concluded these did not materially impact the overall opinion as findings were specific to individual areas rather than suggesting wider control issues.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance indicates control weaknesses in specific areas. While deemed non-material by internal audit, a lender would need to understand whether these issues affect services or assets material to the council's operations or finances.
findings.figures: 2 Limited Assurance out of 23 audits; 9 Substantial, 8 Reasonable, 4 advisory
findings.quote: In respect of the two audits receiving Limited assurance (Old River Lane & Homelessness), we concluded that this did not materially impact on our overall opinion as the related audit findings were specific to the individual area subject to audit, as opposed to suggesting wider control issues across the Council as a whole.

findings.headline: Capital programme historically experienced slippage; management has strengthened oversight but scale is reducing
findings.detail: External auditors recommended strengthening capital programme management and forecasting due to historical slippage. Management has responded by providing more robust oversight through the Asset Management Group. However, the capital programme is now reducing in scale, which management notes 'should support improved deliverability'.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage indicates project delivery management issues. The fact that scale is reducing suggests either a strategic shift or pragmatic recognition of delivery capacity constraints.
findings.figures: Capital programme reducing in scale going forward
findings.quote: More robust challenge and oversight of capital planning, profiling and delivery is being provided through the officer Asset Management Group. It is also noted that the capital programme is reducing in scale going forward, which should support improved deliverability and more realistic forecasting.

findings.headline: BEAM project flagged as key exception requiring contingency pending business plan review
findings.detail: While the council is reducing reliance on reserves for revenue spending, BEAM is identified as 'the key exception'. A contingency remains in place pending the outcome of a business plan review. The statement does not provide detail on what BEAM is or why it requires ongoing contingency.
findings.matters: A named contingency on an identified project signals financial or delivery risk that a lender would want to understand in detail.
findings.figures: BEAM noted as outlier to otherwise improving financial management position
findings.quote: BEAM remains the key exception, with a contingency in place pending the outcome of the business plan review.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will place additional demands on capacity and skills, with risk of losing key staff
findings.detail: External auditors flag that the council must assess whether it has necessary skills and capacity to support Local Government Reorganisation and identify gaps. Management acknowledges that LGR will place additional demands and may increase risk of losing key staff and corporate knowledge. Multiple recommendations emphasise ensuring financial decisions support the future unitary council and maintaining financial resilience through transition.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the council will maintain strong financial governance, reporting capability, and senior staff continuity through local government reorganisation, particularly given the concurrent finance team restructuring.
findings.figures: MTFP extends to 2028/29; reorganisation occurring during this planning period
findings.quote: Management recognises that LGR will place additional demands on capacity and skills and may increase the risk of losing key staff and corporate knowledge. Skills and capacity are being reviewed to identify any gaps, with mitigating actions such as training or temporary support considered where required.

findings.headline: Finance team restructure underway following capacity constraints that delayed accounts
findings.detail: The council approved a restructure of the finance team on 10 February 2026 following a review. Recruitment to vacant posts is progressing, with agency staff providing interim support. Quality assurance improvements include CFO review of draft accounts and weekly oversight meetings. Significantly, the 2024/25 accounts were completed on time 'for the first time in a number of years', indicating prior reporting delays were material.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity directly affects timeliness and quality of financial reporting. Prior delays in accounts completion are a red flag for lenders and the council's own finance director.
findings.figures: Restructure approved 10 February 2026; 2024/25 accounts completed within government timescales 'for the first time in a number of years'
findings.quote: Following a review of the team and service, a proposed restructure was presented to Leadership Team and approved on 10 February. Work is now progressing on recruitment to a number of vacant posts. In the interim, agency staff are supporting where necessary to ensure sufficient capacity within the team

findings.detail: The council has approved asset disposals with the explicit purpose of realising capital receipts to pay down debt. This sits alongside reductions in non-essential capital expenditure. The asset disposal programme is described as 'continuing', indicating this is an active ongoing strategy.

findings.quote: Non‑essential capital expenditure has been reduced, and asset disposals have been approved to realise capital receipts that will be used to pay down debt.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Risk Register Q4 2025/26
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating one-off costs and transition disruption with significant uncertainty on timelines
findings.detail: LGR is classified as a new risk that places significant demands on capacity and may lead to additional one-off costs, service disruption, loss of key staff, and weakened financial resilience. Initial provision for one-off costs has been included in the MTFP, but significant uncertainty remains regarding implementation timelines and final structure. Council is monitoring national policy developments but lacks clarity on when and how the reorganisation will conclude.
findings.matters: Uncertainty on LGR timelines affects medium-term financial forecasting and risk of unexpected costs or service disruption during the transition period represents near-term financial exposure.
findings.figures: Initial provision for one-off costs included in Medium Term Financial Plan (no amount specified)
findings.quote: This may lead to additional one-off costs, disruption to service delivery, loss of key staff, reduced organisational focus on current priorities, and weakened financial resilience during the transition period.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Risk Register Q4 2025/26
findings.headline: Section 114 notice threatened if expenditure continues to exceed funding
findings.detail: The council faces continued reductions in external funding combined with increasing service demand and inflationary pressures that could trigger a Section 114 notice from the s.151 Officer. This would require Commissioner appointment and trigger a formal public interest report. The council is actively seeking CIPFA support ahead of reaching this threshold to strengthen financial oversight. Asset disposals have been approved specifically to pay down debt, and non-essential capital expenditure has been reduced.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice represents formal inability to balance the budget and is a core indicator of financial distress for lenders to local government.
findings.figures: No specific deficit figures disclosed; council is managing to what it calls 'real-terms reductions' in funding
findings.quote: Expenditure exceeds the resources available to the Council, caused by continued reductions in external funding, increasing service demand, and inflationary pressures, which could lead to the s.151 Officer issuing a Section 114(3) notice

findings.headline: New corporate risk added for Local Government Reorganisation with potential for additional one-off costs
findings.detail: East Herts has added Risk 10 to the corporate register to capture financial, governance and service delivery uncertainties from potential local government reorganisation. The council explicitly identifies risks of additional one-off costs, organisational capacity pressure, and service delivery disruption during any transition period.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of potential material costs and organisational capacity constraints that could impact the council's financial position and service resilience
findings.figures: None specified for this risk in the document
findings.quote: The risk captures the financial, governance and service delivery uncertainties associated with LGR, including the potential for additional one-off costs, pressure on organisational capacity, and disruption to service delivery during any transition period.

findings.headline: Multiple capital projects reclassified to revenue treatment, affecting capital programme reporting.
findings.detail: Hertford Castle Grounds development and some UKSPF schemes have been switched from capital to revenue accounting during 2025/26. This changes how their performance is measured against the capital programme.
findings.matters: Reclassifications can mask capital programme performance and affect comparability year-on-year.

findings.headline: Hertford Theatre S278 outstanding works of £81k remain uncosted.
findings.detail: The council notes £81k of committed Section 278 infrastructure works that are outstanding and not yet invoiced. Costs are unknown but the council says they should stay within budget.
findings.matters: Unpriced committed expenditure creates cost uncertainty on a live project and affects year-end position.
findings.figures: Outstanding S278 works £81k
findings.quote: Outstanding S278 works (£81k). Figures not yet known but should still be within budget.

findings.headline: Buntingford depot EV infrastructure planning application rejected; alternatives being sought.
findings.detail: The planned structural changes at Amwell as part of the depot EV infrastructure work failed planning. The council is now pursuing unspecified alternative opportunities, introducing uncertainty and likely delay.
findings.matters: Failed planning and need for alternatives signals project risk, cost pressure (alternatives may be more expensive), and delivery delay.
findings.figures: Additional £10k contingency was spent at Buntingford; Amwell alternative still undefined
findings.quote: Planning application for structural changes at Amwell was unsuccessful. Officers to seek alternatives opportunities.

findings.headline: BEAM website replacement went £9k over budget despite delivery.
findings.detail: The new website was launched in early February 2026 but exceeded its £51k budget. This is an explicit cost overrun on a completed project.
findings.matters: Indicates cost control issues on capital projects, which affects predictability of future scheme costs.
findings.figures: Budget £51k, Outturn £51k plus £9k over
findings.quote: Outturn is £9k over budget.

findings.detail: The revised budget was £11.925m; outturn was £8.628m, leaving £3.297m unspent. An additional £1.142m is carried into 2026/27. The shortfall represents material slippage across multiple project categories.
findings.matters: Large underspends raise questions about delivery capability, project planning, and the council's ability to execute its capital strategy on schedule.
findings.figures: Budget £11,925k, Outturn £8,628k, Variance (£3,297k), Carry Forward £1,142k

findings.detail: The budget assumed using £164k of earmarked reserves to balance the position. Actual usage was £1,360k — an additional £1,196k drawdown not provided for. This represents a one-off consumption of accumulated reserves to mask an underlying operating deficit.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund operating expenditure is unsustainable and reduces financial flexibility for future years. When combined with the Net Cost of Services overspend of £2,405k, it shows the council's underlying position is worse than the headline year-end surplus suggests.
findings.figures: Budgeted reserve use £164k, actual use £1,360k, unbudgeted drawdown £1,196k

findings.headline: Unforecasted property fund loss of £448k in the final quarter
findings.detail: The outturn shows a loss on property funds of £448k that does not appear in any Q3 forecast line. This was entirely a fourth-quarter movement, suggesting either sudden investment losses or a revaluation that was not anticipated.
findings.matters: Unforecasted investment losses indicate either inadequate investment oversight or unexpected market deterioration affecting the council's capital portfolio. This erodes reserves and raises questions about asset management.
findings.figures: £448k loss entirely unbudgeted and unforecasted
